 Seniors Ignoring Plan Termination Letters Could Start 2027 Without Drug Coverage as 3.2 Million Lose Medicare Advantage Plans
 Published Oct 26, 2026 10:30 AM EDT 
 By
 Dorothy Brooks 
 Kampus Production | Pexels 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 Nearly 3.2 million Medicare Advantage enrollees , almost 11% of the total, must find new coverage for 2027 because their insurers are no longer offering their plans, according to a Medicare Market Insights review of federal data reported by CNN . More than 1 million people in stand-alone Part D drug plans are also losing their plans, according to consulting firm Oliver Wyman. With open enrollment ending Dec. 7, the costliest mistake for many of these households may be the simplest one: doing nothing.
 A member whose Medicare Advantage plan ends and who takes no action is generally moved to Original Medicare on Jan. 1. That keeps hospital and doctor coverage in place, but it does not include prescription drug coverage unless the person joins a separate Part D plan. For a parent who relies on insulin or a blood thinner, that gap can surface at the pharmacy counter in early January.
 Insurers send these termination letters, known as nonrenewal notices, before open enrollment begins. Adult children and caregivers who help manage an older relative's mail may be the first to spot them.
 A Third Straight Year of Plan Cancellations
 About 2.9 million enrollees lost plans for 2026 and about 2 million for 2025, compared with the 1% to 2% who typically lost plans in earlier years, said Jared Strock, founder of Medicare Market Insights. Humana, UnitedHealthcare, Aetna and several Blue Cross Blue Shield carriers are among the insurers cutting plans or leaving areas, and many of the canceled plans are preferred provider organization, or PPO, policies.
 Rural areas are feeling it most. A KFF analysis found that about 638,000 beneficiaries in 193 counties will have no Medicare Advantage drug plan available for general enrollment in 2027, up from 399,000 people in 123 counties this year. Aetna is also leaving the stand-alone Part D market in about half of states, Oliver Wyman said.
 MedicalDaily previously reported that members facing 2027 plan exits should check doctor networks before open enrollment begins. Since then, the scale of the cancellations has come into focus, and the window to act has narrowed to about six weeks.
 The Drug Coverage Gap Behind a Missed Deadline
 People whose plans are ending get extra time. They can switch during open enrollment or use a special enrollment period that runs from Dec. 8 through the last day of February, according to the Washington state insurance commissioner's office . But a new plan starts on the first day of the month after the person switches, so waiting into January can mean weeks of paying full price for prescriptions.
 A longer lapse can cost more. Medicare may add a late enrollment penalty to a Part D premium when someone goes 63 or more days in a row without Part D or other creditable drug coverage, and the surcharge generally lasts as long as the person has Part D. People who get Extra Help do not pay the penalty.
 Costs are rising even for those who act. No stand-alone Part D plan will offer a $0 premium in 2027 for people without low-income help, the standard deductible will rise from $615 to $700, and the yearly out-of-pocket cap will climb from $2,100 to $2,400, Straight Arrow News reported , citing KFF.
 Timothy McBride, a health policy analyst and professor at Washington University in St. Louis, urged enrollees to weigh "not just the premium, but also things like the deductible and the caps," he told ABC News . Mary Beth Donahue, CEO of the Better Medicare Alliance, said in a statement to CNN, "Seniors shouldn't have to face this disruption every year." 
 The people most exposed include those who take several or high-cost medications, rural residents with fewer replacement plans, and older adults who live alone or have memory problems. Former PPO members may also face narrower doctor networks in a new plan.
 Steps to Take Before Dec. 7
 Start by finding the letter and keeping it as proof that the plan is ending. Then list every prescription, dose, pharmacy, and regular doctor.
 Compare plans on Medicare.gov's Plan Finder or by calling 1-800-MEDICARE. Free counseling is available through each state's State Health Insurance Assistance Program, or SHIP, and people with limited income should ask about Extra Help.
 Anyone who runs short of an essential medication during a coverage change should contact the prescriber or pharmacist rather than skip doses. Be wary of unsolicited calls: Medicare will not call unexpectedly to ask for a Medicare number.
 Coverage chosen during open enrollment begins Jan. 1, and people already in a Medicare Advantage plan can make one change from Jan. 1 to March 31. CMS has not yet released its overview of 2027 supplemental benefits, such as dental and hearing coverage.
 A short review with a family member or SHIP counselor before Dec. 7 is the simplest way to avoid starting 2027 without drug coverage.

 Key Questions Answered
 What happens if my Medicare Advantage plan ends and I do nothing? You will generally be moved to Original Medicare on Jan. 1. You will not have Part D drug coverage unless you enroll in a drug plan.
 How many people are losing their plans for 2027? About 3.2 million Medicare Advantage members and more than 1 million stand-alone Part D members.
 What is the deadline to choose a new plan? Open enrollment ends Dec. 7. People whose plans are ending also have a special enrollment period from Dec. 8 through Feb. 28, 2027.
 Is there a penalty for going without drug coverage? Medicare may charge a late enrollment penalty after 63 or more days in a row without creditable drug coverage. People who get Extra Help do not pay it.
 Where can seniors get free help? Call 1-800-MEDICARE, use Medicare.gov's Plan Finder, or contact your state's SHIP program.
